advances: For every orbit cutoff in a balanced ternary layer and every individual spatial affine weight, the actual first-depth average has the absolute scale \(2^{-k}\). The proof supplies the previously unsupported dimension-linear energy-variance estimate for weighted balanced signs by conditioning independent Bernoulli variables at their mean. Together with parity chains and reflection, this gives an actual third-depth moment of scale \(8^{-k}\) by Jensen. This is a theorem for the stated balanced truncated layers, not a proof of the general locked conjecture.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The Bernoulli conditioning estimates, coefficient log-concavity, covariance calculation, and energy-variance bound are proved above. The Boolean chain construction, central-binomial estimate, and Gaussian Fourier identity are the explicitly identified elementary ingredients from accepted fact \(\texttt{98175b11f4e453f3}\).
proof:
We first prove the energy-variance estimate needed for the parity classes. We give its details because the coordinate dependence imposed by balance prevents the independent-coordinate argument from applying directly.

Consider independent Bernoulli variables \(B_1,\ldots,B_L\) with parameters \(\rho_i\in(0,1)\), where \(L\ge2\) and \(\sum_i\rho_i=q\) is an integer with \(1\le q\le L-1\). Write \(S=\sum_iB_i\), and let \(\widehat B\) have their conditional law given \(S=q\). Put \(\pi_i=\mathbb P(\widehat B_i=1)\). We will show

$$
\pi_i\le3\rho_i,\qquad
1-\pi_i\le3(1-\rho_i),\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat B_i,\widehat B_j)\le0\quad(i\ne j).
\tag{1}
$$

Here is an elementary log-concavity observation used twice below. A nonnegative sequence \((f_j)\), positive on a contiguous finite interval and zero elsewhere, is log-concave if \(f_j^2\ge f_{j-1}f_{j+1}\). Its positive successive ratios then decrease. Convolution with a two-term positive sequence preserves this property: for \(g_j=u f_j+v f_{j-1}\), where \(u,v>0\), expansion gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_j^2-g_{j-1}g_{j+1}
={}&u^2(f_j^2-f_{j-1}f_{j+1})
+v^2(f_{j-1}^2-f_{j-2}f_j)\\
&+uv(f_jf_{j-1}-f_{j-2}f_{j+1})\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$

The last term is nonnegative by decreasing ratios whenever its right product is positive, and otherwise by nonnegativity. The same argument covers the endpoints of the support. Starting with a singleton sequence, induction proves log-concavity both for Poisson-binomial probability masses and for the coefficients of any product \(\prod_i(1+t_i x)\) with \(t_i>0\).

Fix \(i\), put \(T=S-B_i\), and let \(f_j=\mathbb P(T=j)\). These masses are positive for \(0\le j\le L-1\) and log-concave. Define \(R=f_{q-1}/f_q>0\). Independence gives
\(\pi_i=\rho_iR/(1-\rho_i+\rho_iR)\). If \(R\le1\), then \(\pi_i\le\rho_i\). Suppose \(R>1\). All successive ratios in the tail beginning at \(q-1\) are at most \(R^{-1}\). Consequently the nonnegative integer variable \(T-(q-1)\), conditional on \(T\ge q-1\), has tail probabilities satisfying
\(\mathbb P(T-(q-1)\ge h\mid T\ge q-1)\le R^{-h}\) for every integer \(h\ge0\). To see this directly, shift the finite sum defining each tail by one index and use the bound \(f_{j+1}\le R^{-1}f_j\). Summing these tail bounds gives

$$
\mathbb E[T\mid T\ge q-1]
\le q-1+\sum_{h\ge1}R^{-h}
=q-1+\frac1{R-1}.
$$

Conditioning on this upper tail can only increase the mean, so
\(q-\rho_i=\mathbb ET\le q-1+1/(R-1)\). It follows that \(R\le1+1/(1-\rho_i)\). If \(\rho_i\le1/2\), this is \(R\le3\), and the formula for \(\pi_i\) gives \(\pi_i/\rho_i\le R\le3\), since its denominator is at least one. If \(\rho_i>1/2\), the bound \(\pi_i\le1<2\rho_i\) suffices. This proves the first inequality in (1). Apply the same argument to the independent variables \(1-B_i\), whose mean sum is the integer \(L-q\), to prove the second.

For the covariance assertion, put \(t_i=\rho_i/(1-\rho_i)>0\). The conditional law is proportional to \(\prod_{i:b_i=1}t_i\) on the \(q\)-subsets. For distinct \(i,j\), write \(e_h\) for the elementary symmetric sum of degree \(h\) in the remaining \(L-2\) positive weights, with \(e_0=1\) and \(e_h=0\) outside \(0\le h\le L-2\). Its normalizer is
\(C=e_q+(t_i+t_j)e_{q-1}+t_it_je_{q-2}>0\). Direct expansion yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi_i&=\frac{t_i(e_{q-1}+t_je_{q-2})}{C},\qquad
\pi_j=\frac{t_j(e_{q-1}+t_ie_{q-2})}{C},\\
\pi_i\pi_j-\mathbb P(\widehat B_i=\widehat B_j=1)
&=\frac{t_it_j}{C^2}(e_{q-1}^2-e_qe_{q-2})\ge0.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last inequality follows from (2) applied to the elementary symmetric coefficient sequence; the zero conventions include \(q=1\) and \(q=L-1\). Thus (1) is proved.

Since \(\sum_i\widehat B_i=q\) is constant, every row of its covariance matrix sums to zero. Write \(c_{ij}=-\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat B_i,\widehat B_j)\ge0\) for \(i\ne j\). For arbitrary real \(a_i\), (1) gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_i a_i\widehat B_i\right)
&=\sum_{i<j}c_{ij}(a_i-a_j)^2\\
&\le2\sum_i a_i^2\pi_i(1-\pi_i)
\le12\sum_i a_i^2\rho_i(1-\rho_i).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$

Indeed, \(\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\le\min\{\pi_i,1-\pi_i\}\le3\min\{\rho_i,1-\rho_i\}\le6\rho_i(1-\rho_i)\).

Now fix an even set \(E\subseteq[k]\) with \(L=|E|=2q\ge2\), and let \(\xi\in\{-1,1\}^E\) have probabilities proportional to \(e^{-\sum_{i\in E}\beta_i\xi_i}\) subject to \(\sum_{i\in E}\xi_i=0\). There is a unique \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) for which
\(\sum_{i\in E}(1+e^{2(\beta_i-\lambda)})^{-1}=q\): the left side is continuous, strictly increasing in \(\lambda\), and ranges from zero to \(L\). Set \(a_i=2(\beta_i-\lambda)\) and \(\rho_i=(1+e^{a_i})^{-1}\). Then \((\xi_i+1)/2\) has exactly the conditional Bernoulli law just studied. The conditioning fixes its sum at \(q\), so \(\sum_i\beta_i\xi_i\) and \(\sum_i a_i\widehat B_i\) differ by the constant \(2\lambda q-\sum_i\beta_i\). Further,
\(a_i^2\rho_i(1-\rho_i)=a_i^2/(4\cosh^2(a_i/2))\le1\), because \(\cosh u\ge1+u^2/2\ge|u|\). Therefore (3) proves the uniform bound

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\beta\cdot\xi)\le12|E|.
\tag{4}
$$

For \(E=\varnothing\), the energy is the constant zero and (4) holds as well. This proof uses the fixed-cardinality product structure, not a varentropy assertion for general complete convex supports.

We turn to the original support. Write \(\mathbf1=(1,\ldots,1)\). A point \(I\in D\) has centered vector \(I-\mathbf1\in\{-1,0,1\}^k\) of coordinate sum zero and support size at most \(2r\). Its number of positive and negative centered coordinates is equal. Thus its parity class is specified by the even-cardinality set \(E=\{i:I_i\ne1\}\). Conversely every balanced sign assignment on every even set \(E\) of size at most \(2r\) occurs. Let

$$
V_E=\sum_{\substack{I\in D\\\{i:I_i\ne1\}=E}}w_I,
\qquad
Q_{\mathrm{par}}=\sum_{\substack{E\subseteq[k]\\|E|\text{ even},\ |E|\le2r}}V_E^2.
$$

These are masses of the original weight table, so \(Z=\sum_E V_E\). If \(E'=E\cup\{a,b\}\) for distinct \(a,b\notin E\), extend each balanced assignment on \(E\) by the centered values \((1,-1)\) and \((-1,1)\) on \((a,b)\). These are distinct members of the parity class \(E'\). Their original weight ratios to the original assignment are \(e^{-\beta_a+\beta_b}\) and \(e^{\beta_a-\beta_b}\), respectively. Hence
\(V_{E'}\ge2\cosh(\beta_a-\beta_b)V_E\ge2V_E\).

Accepted fact \(\texttt{98175b11f4e453f3}\) proves that the Boolean lattice on \(k\) coordinates has a symmetric-chain partition with \(\binom{k}{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}\) chains, and that this number is at most \(2^k/\sqrt{k+1}\). Here its dimension \(n\) is the present \(k\). We use those Boolean combinatorial statements and its Gaussian identity below. Its scalar letter \(A\) and its ternary weight normalizer \(W\) are not used: the present \(A\) is the support \(D\times\{0\}\), and all masses here are the original \(w_I\) and \(Z\).

Retain from each Boolean chain only its even levels of cardinality at most \(2r\). This gives a possibly empty chain whose successive sets differ by two coordinates. Along a nonempty retained chain the masses \(u_1,\ldots,u_l\) satisfy \(u_{j+1}\ge2u_j\), so
\((\sum_j u_j)^2\le3\sum_j u_j^2\): expand the square and use \(\sum_{i<j}u_i\le u_j\sum_{h\ge1}2^{-h}\le u_j\). Cauchy-Schwarz over the Boolean chains now gives

$$
Z^2\le3\binom{k}{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}Q_{\mathrm{par}},
\qquad
Q_{\mathrm{par}}\ge\frac{\sqrt{k+1}}{3\,2^k}Z^2.
\tag{5}
$$

For \(J\in D\), define \(\tau_w(J)=Z\tau_p((J,0))\) and the oriented reflected sum

$$
S_J=\sum_{\substack{v\in\mathbb Z^k\\J+v\in D,\ J-v\in D}}
\min\{w_{J+v},w_{J-v}\}.
$$

Every closed ambient halfspace containing \((J,0)\) contains at least one of \((J+v,0)\) and \((J-v,0)\), since their midpoint is \((J,0)\). This is valid for every ambient normal, including pure height normals. Sum the corresponding minimum-weight inequality over the oriented \(v\). Each reflected endpoint is counted twice on the mass side, including \(v=0\), and the resulting reflected mass in the halfspace is bounded above by its original total mass. Taking the infimum gives \(\tau_w(J)\ge S_J/2\), and therefore

$$
\sum_{J\in D}p_{(J,0)}\tau_p((J,0))
\ge\frac1{2Z^2}\sum_{J\in D}w_JS_J.
\tag{6}
$$

The map \((J,v)\mapsto(I,K)=(J+v,J-v)\) is a bijection onto the ordered pairs of original points having the same parity. For the converse, their midpoint is integral and ternary, has centered coordinate sum zero, and its centered support is contained in the common parity support \(E\); thus its number of twos is at most \(|E|/2\le r\), so the midpoint belongs to \(D\). Log-affinity gives \(w_Iw_K=w_J^2\) and
\(w_J\min\{w_I,w_K\}=w_Iw_K e^{-|\beta\cdot(I-K)/2|}\). Consequently

$$
\sum_{J\in D}w_JS_J
=\sum_E V_E^2\,\mathbb E e^{-|T_E|},
\qquad T_E=\beta\cdot(X-Y)/2,
\tag{7}
$$

where \(X,Y\) are independent original endpoints from the parity class \(E\), each sampled with probabilities \(w_I/V_E\). On that class \(X-\mathbf1\) is the weighted balanced-sign vector of (4). The constant translation of the energy does not affect its variance. Independence thus gives \(\mathbb E T_E=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T_E)=\operatorname{Var}(\beta\cdot X)/2\le6|E|\le6k\).

Although the coordinates of \(X\) are dependent, the characteristic function of \(T_E\) is nonnegative everywhere:
\(\mathbb E e^{itT_E}=|\mathbb E e^{it\beta\cdot X/2}|^2\ge0\). It is real and equals \(\mathbb E\cos(tT_E)\). Since \(\cos u\ge1-u^2/2\), it is at least \(1-3kt^2\). The Gaussian Fourier identity proved in accepted fact \(\texttt{98175b11f4e453f3}\) is
\(e^{-z^2}=\pi^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-s^2}\cos(2sz)\,ds\).
Apply it to the finite law of \(T_E\). Nonnegativity of its characteristic function permits restricting the integral to \(|s|\le1/\sqrt{24k}\), where the characteristic function at \(2s\) is at least \(1/2\). This proves

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E e^{-T_E^2}
&\ge\frac1{\sqrt\pi}\int_{-1/\sqrt{24k}}^{1/\sqrt{24k}}
e^{-s^2}\frac12\,ds
\ge\frac{e^{-1/24}}{2\sqrt{6\pi}\sqrt k},\\
\mathbb E e^{-|T_E|}
&\ge e^{-1/4}\mathbb E e^{-T_E^2}
\ge\frac{e^{-7/24}}{2\sqrt{6\pi}\sqrt k}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
$$

The second line uses \((|z|-1/2)^2\ge0\), or \(e^{-|z|}\ge e^{-1/4}e^{-z^2}\). Empty parity support gives \(T_E=0\) and is included.

Combining (5)-(8) yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{J\in D}p_{(J,0)}\tau_p((J,0))
&\ge\frac{e^{-7/24}}{4\sqrt{6\pi}\sqrt k}
\frac{Q_{\mathrm{par}}}{Z^2}\\
&\ge\frac{e^{-7/24}}{12\sqrt{6\pi}}
\sqrt{\frac{k+1}{k}}\,2^{-k}
\ge c\,2^{-k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, Jensen's inequality for the original probability law \(p\) and the convex function \(t\mapsto t^3\) on \([0,\infty)\) gives the claimed bound on \(M_3(p)\). The argument includes \(r=0\), \(k=1\), and all lower-dimensional affine supports.
statement:
Let \(k\ge1\) and \(0\le r\le\lfloor k/2\rfloor\) be integers. For arbitrary \(\beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_k)\in\mathbb R^k\), define

$$
\begin{aligned}
D&=\left\{I\in\{0,1,2\}^k:
\sum_{i=1}^k I_i=k,\quad \#\{i:I_i=2\}\le r\right\},\\
A&=D\times\{0\}\subseteq\mathbb R^{k+1},\qquad
w_I=e^{-\beta\cdot I},\qquad
Z=\sum_{I\in D}w_I,\qquad
p_{(I,0)}=w_I/Z.
\end{aligned}
$$

For \(J\in D\), let \(\tau_p((J,0))\) be the infimum of the original probability mass of \(A\cap H\) over all closed affine halfspaces \(H\subseteq\mathbb R^{k+1}\) containing \((J,0)\), with nonzero normal, including normals with a height component. Set \(c=e^{-7/24}/(12\sqrt{6\pi})\). Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{J\in D}p_{(J,0)}\tau_p((J,0))&\ge c\,2^{-k},\\
M_3(p):=\sum_{J\in D}p_{(J,0)}\tau_p((J,0))^3&\ge c^3\,8^{-k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

All normalizers, sampling probabilities, and halfspace masses in these inequalities belong to the original affine weight table. No equality of the individual \(\beta_i\) is assumed.
